n0001.title: A Theory of Bugs
n0001.gist: Bugs are inevitable because computational irreducibility makes even simple programs do things no finite check can foresee.
n0001.question: Bugs — why can't any program be guaranteed free of them? (a theoretical account)
n0001.sourceHeading: Towards a Theory of Bugs: The Ruliology of the Unexpected

n0002.title: Introduction
n0002.gist: Even very simple programs already show the unpredictable behavior we call bugs, because their computation can be as sophisticated as any system, following the Principle of Computational Equivalence.
n0002.question: Bugs — can a general theory explain why they occur? (a research program outlined)

n0003.title: Title and Byline
n0003.gist: An essay title, reading-time note, and blank spacer precede the discussion.
n0003.sourceHeading: Towards a Theory of Bugs: The Ruliology of the Unexpected

n0007.title: “My Program Did the Wrong Thing!”
n0007.gist: Bugs are unexpected departures from a simple mental model of what a program should do, and they arise because even simple programs can compute with full sophistication, producing irreducible surprises no automated system can fully foresee.

n0015.title: Bugs in Turing Machines
n0015.gist: Simple three- and four-state Turing machines built to compute n+1 reveal bugs at specific inputs like 7, 15, or 63, showing that errors can lurk arbitrarily far into a program's behavior.
n0015.question: Turing machines — how far must one test before a bug appears? (several worked examples)

n0016.title: Discovering the First Bug
n0016.gist: A simple Turing machine built to compute n+1 appears correct for small inputs, but testing input 7 reveals it outputs 9 instead of 8, exposing a hidden bug.

n0025.title: Mapping the Glitches
n0025.gist: Plotting the machine's outputs shows a repeating pattern of errors at inputs of the form 8k minus 1, traced to extra incorrect moves the head makes when the input's binary digits end in 111.

n0030.title: How Many Machines Get It Right
n0030.gist: Among thousands of small Turing machines that correctly compute n+1, some operate simply while others look deceptively complex, and bugs can first appear only after testing many inputs.

n0039.title: Insidious Bugs in Larger Machines
n0039.gist: Larger machines can run correctly for dozens of inputs before suddenly failing, with the hardest-to-find bugs concentrated at inputs whose binary digits are all ones, growing rarer as machines get bigger.

n0052.title: What Counts as a Bug?
n0052.gist: Whether a program "has a bug" depends on comparing it to some simpler specification, and tests on Turing machines show that almost any specification one proposes will eventually be violated.
n0052.question: Specifications — what kinds of rules can define a bug, and do any escape violation? (several specification types tested)

n0053.title: Specifications Define Bugs
n0053.gist: A program always just does what it does; calling something a bug requires comparing it against a simpler specification, such as restating the program in another language or form.

n0057.title: Comparing Equivalent Programs
n0057.gist: Two Turing machines that appear to compute the same function instead diverge at input 27, and the resulting pattern of where they disagree turns out to be surprisingly complicated.

n0064.title: Specifying What Shouldn't Happen
n0064.gist: Machines that seem to compute happily can suddenly go out of control, expanding their memory use forever or falling into an infinite loop, violating a specification that merely forbids such behavior.

n0075.title: No Escape from Insidious Bugs
n0075.gist: Even a specification as simple as requiring even-numbered output is eventually violated, suggesting that whatever constraint is imposed, some machine will seem to satisfy it until it insidiously fails.

n0081.title: Cellular Automaton Examples
n0081.gist: Cellular automata built to double their input size show the same pattern as Turing machines—apparent correctness that later fails—though in some cases a structural argument can prove no bug will ever occur.
n0081.question: Cellular automata — can one tell in advance whether a rule will eventually bug out? (two cases analyzed in depth)

n0082.title: A Cellular Automaton Example
n0082.gist: Cellular automata designed so that n cells become 2n cells generally work, but some rules that seem to double correctly instead fail unexpectedly at inputs such as 14, 24, or 32.

n0096.title: When Is a Bug Visually Obvious
n0096.gist: Some cellular automaton patterns are visually simple enough to guarantee no bug, but others that look similarly complex can run without error for 100,000 steps while still showing unpredictable, seemingly random fluctuations.

n0109.title: A Second Uncertain Case
n0109.gist: A further cellular automaton again shows roughly linear but randomly fluctuating stabilization times, leaving open whether its pattern will ever escape containment, until the full process of computation is examined directly.

n0118.title: Proving No Bugs Occur
n0118.gist: Analyzing the cellular automaton's inner "rind" and the simplified rule it obeys shows the pattern can never expand or loop forever, proving the doubling rule always works despite its complex appearance.

n0132.title: But What about Formal Proofs?
n0132.gist: Representing Turing machine tapes and rules as symbolic expressions lets one construct formal, inductive proofs that certain machines always compute n+1 correctly, but no such proof exists for a machine that actually has a bug.
n0132.question: Formal proofs — can symbolic logic certify a program is bug-free? (a worked proof and its limits)

n0133.title: Setting Up a Proof
n0133.gist: Testing a Turing machine on many inputs strongly suggests it always computes n+1, but confirming this for every possible input requires moving from observation to an actual formal proof.

n0140.title: A Symbolic Representation
n0140.gist: Representing the tape as a run-length-encoded linked list with symbolic markers for the head's position lets the Turing machine's rules be rewritten as algebraic-like axioms suitable for formal manipulation.

n0159.title: Proving Correctness by Induction
n0159.gist: Using automated equational proof search together with mathematical induction, one can derive a finite symbolic proof that a machine always computes n+1, and this method extends to other small bug-free machines.

n0170.title: Why No Proof Exists for Bugs
n0170.gist: Proofs correspond to paths through a graph of derivable theorems, and for a machine with a genuine bug no such path exists because the statement is simply false, so finding the bug still takes unbounded effort.

n0184.title: Irreducibility, Induction, and Surprises
n0184.gist: Because computational irreducibility is everywhere, no finite method—testing, sampling, or scientific induction—can guarantee that a program's behavior hides no rare, arbitrarily buried bug.
n0184.question: Irreducibility — why can't testing or scientific reasoning ever rule out bugs for good? (several lines of argument)

n0185.title: Computational Irreducibility and Bugs
n0185.gist: Bugs ultimately stem from computational irreducibility, the fact that a system's behavior can only be known by running it, so any bounded amount of checking can always be surprised, even though pockets of predictability always exist too.

n0196.title: The Failure of Ruliological Induction
n0196.gist: Scientific induction, which assumes a pattern seen many times will always hold, fails for computationally irreducible systems because bugs can be made arbitrarily rare, so testing—however extensive or randomized—may never find them.
n0196.sourceHeading: Did I Test Enough Cases? The Failure of Ruliological Induction

n0208.title: Some Typical Ruliological Surprises
n0208.gist: Across cellular automata, Turing machines, combinators, and multiway systems, decades of exploring simple rules repeatedly turn up unexpected behavior, confirming that surprises—bugs relative to expectation—are the rule rather than the exception in the computational universe.

n0240.title: Bugs in Mathematics and Practice
n0240.gist: Mathematics mostly avoids ruliology-style bugs by focusing on humanly understandable structure, while writing genuinely bug-resistant software depends on well-designed languages and on visualizing what programs actually do.
n0240.question: Mathematics and practice — how do humans manage to limit, if not eliminate, bugs? (examples from math and language design)

n0241.title: Mathematical “Bugs”
n0241.gist: Mathematical hypotheses can also fail unexpectedly, as with polynomial coefficients or prime-counting patterns that break only after astronomically many cases, yet pure mathematics avoids such surprises by concentrating on humanly tractable structure rather than raw computation.

n0256.title: Bugs in Practice
n0256.gist: Avoiding bugs in practice depends on well-designed language primitives that match human intent and on visualizing what a program actually does inside, though any program doing genuinely irreducible computation retains some chance of unexpected behavior.

n0274.title: Thanks
n0274.gist: Acknowledgments thank Wolfram Institute colleagues and the Wolfram Software Quality Assurance team for help and for shaping decades of intuition about bugs.
